```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(".."))   # run from project root
library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2); library(lubridate); library(MASS)
select <- dplyr::select   # MASS masks select()
```

## Goal

Score candidate models on data they have not seen, and pick one.

## Criteria (and why)

| Metric | Meaning | Role |
|----|----|----|
| **Negative log-likelihood (log score)** on test data | how much probability the model gave to what happened; penalises overconfidence | **primary** |
| Poisson deviance | generalised squared error for counts | secondary |
| MAE of annual beach totals | average miss in incidents per beach per year; easy to explain | secondary |
| Predicted / actual total | calibration: are we right in total? | check |
| Severe only: top-10 beach capture | share of actual severe incidents that fall in the 10 beaches we ranked highest (random = 12.5%) | check |
| AIC / BIC | in-sample fit, penalised for size | tie-breaker only |

**Why time-based:** the forecast is for the *future*, so we test on the
future. Random splits leak (same beach, adjacent months).

**One caveat for all scores here:** the test rows use the *actual*
visitors, weather and safety hours of the test year. In the real
forecast (step 06) those inputs are assumed, so the real error will be
larger. Step 06 checks how much larger.

```{r load}
panel_f <- readRDS("part1/panel_f.rds")

# "Same as last year" benchmark needs each beach's count 12 months earlier
panel_f <- panel_f %>% arrange(beach_nm, month_date) %>% group_by(beach_nm) %>%
  mutate(across(c(n_all, n_mild, n_cc, n_sev), ~ lag(.x, 12), .names = "{.col}_ly")) %>%
  ungroup()
```

## 1. Single split first

Train: months before Sep 2025 (FY2017 to FY2025, 8,640 rows). Test: Sep
2025 to Aug 2026 (FY2026, 960 rows = 80 beaches x 12 months).

```{r split}
train <- panel_f %>% filter(month_date <  as.Date("2025-09-01"))
test  <- panel_f %>% filter(month_date >= as.Date("2025-09-01"))
c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))
test %>% summarise(across(c(n_all, n_mild, n_cc, n_sev), sum))   # what actually happened
```

The test year had 3,690 incidents: 3,371 mild, 293 close calls and 26
severe. The 26 severe incidents are the most in any year since FY2018,
so the test year is a hard one for severe incidents.

## 2. Scoring functions

All four functions take the actual counts `y` and the predicted means
`mu` for the 960 test rows.

```{r score}
# Log score: average negative log-probability the NB gave to each observed count.
# theta = Inf is the Poisson limit (used for the benchmark, which has no dispersion).
nll_nb <- function(y, mu, theta) {
  if (is.infinite(theta)) mean(-dpois(y, mu, log = TRUE))
  else mean(-dnbinom(y, mu = mu, size = theta, log = TRUE))
}

# Poisson deviance: 2 * sum of y*log(y/mu) - (y - mu); zero when mu = y everywhere
dev_pois <- function(y, mu) 2 * sum(ifelse(y == 0, 0, y * log(y / mu)) - (y - mu))

# Add up each beach's 12 months first, then average the absolute miss over the 80 beaches
mae_beach_year <- function(y, mu, beach) mean(abs(tapply(y, beach, sum) - tapply(mu, beach, sum)))

# Rank beaches by predicted total, take the 10 highest, share of actual incidents they hold
top10_capture <- function(y, mu, beach) {
  a <- tapply(y, beach, sum); p <- tapply(mu, beach, sum)
  sum(a[order(-p)[1:10]]) / sum(a)
}

score <- function(y, mu, theta, beach) c(
  nll = nll_nb(y, mu, theta), dev = dev_pois(y, mu), mae = mae_beach_year(y, mu, beach),
  ratio = sum(mu) / sum(y), top10 = top10_capture(y, mu, beach))
```

Why the log score is the main criterion: the forecast hands Task 2 a
*distribution* of incidents, not just a point. The log score is the only
metric here that checks the spread as well as the centre. A model that
is right on average but far too sure of itself gets punished each time
an unlikely count turns up.

## 3. Compare candidate models

Each candidate adds one block of predictors to the one before, so the
table shows what each block buys out of sample. Two variants test the
open questions from step 04:

-   `v` versions replace `offset(log(visitors))` with `log_visitors` as
    a normal term, so the data choose the exponent (EDA slope about
    0.9).
-   `M6` replaces the five fixed beach traits with one dummy per beach
    (`factor(beach_nm)`). It learns each beach's own level, including
    anything about the beach that we have not measured. The visitor mix
    (`surfer_prop`, `tourist_ratio`) changes month to month, so it
    stays.
-   `S_small` is the small severe model from step 04.

```{r specs}
time   <- c("mon", "period_2021")
cond   <- c("swell_max_m", "wind_days", "rain_mm", "air_temp_hi", "marine_health")
safety <- c("log_lg", "log_drone", "campaign_idx", "first_aid_cap", "pa_system", "flags", "equip_rating")
mix    <- c("surfer_prop", "tourist_ratio")
traits <- c("rips_per_km", "rocky", "fishing", "rockpool", "shore_len_m")

specs <- list(
  M1_visitors = list(rhs = "1"),                                   # offset + intercept only
  M2_season   = list(rhs = time),
  M3_cond     = list(rhs = c(time, cond)),
  M4_safety   = list(rhs = c(time, cond, safety)),
  M5_traits   = list(rhs = c(time, cond, safety, mix, traits)),    # = the step 04 model
  M5v_slope   = list(rhs = c(time, cond, safety, mix, traits, "log_visitors"), offset = FALSE),
  M6_beachFE  = list(rhs = c(time, cond, safety, mix, "factor(beach_nm)")),
  M6v_FEslope = list(rhs = c(time, cond, safety, mix, "factor(beach_nm)", "log_visitors"), offset = FALSE),
  S_small     = list(rhs = c("log_lg", "log_drone", "campaign_idx", "air_temp_hi", "swell_max_m", "period_2021"))
)

make_f <- function(y, s) as.formula(paste(
  y, "~", paste(s$rhs, collapse = " + "),
  if (isFALSE(s$offset)) "" else "+ offset(log(visitors))"))

# Fit every spec on `train` for response y, score on `test`, plus the "same as last year" benchmark
run_split <- function(train, test, y) {
  fits <- lapply(names(specs), function(nm) {
    m <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(glm.nb(make_f(y, specs[[nm]]), data = train)),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(m)) return(NULL)
    mu <- predict(m, test, type = "response")
    data.frame(model = nm, t(score(test[[y]], mu, m$theta, test$beach_nm)), AIC = AIC(m), BIC = BIC(m))
  })
  # benchmark: same beach, same month, last year; floored at 0.1 so a zero last year
  # does not give probability 0 to any incident this year
  ly <- pmax(test[[paste0(y, "_ly")]], 0.1)
  bench <- data.frame(model = "B0_lastyear", t(score(test[[y]], ly, Inf, test$beach_nm)), AIC = NA, BIC = NA)
  bind_rows(bench, fits)
}

sev_names <- c(n_mild = "Mild", n_cc = "Close call", n_sev = "Severe", n_all = "All")
single <- bind_rows(lapply(names(sev_names), function(y) run_split(train, test, y) %>% mutate(y = y)))
```

```{r single_tables, results = "asis"}
for (y in names(sev_names)) {
  print(knitr::kable(single %>% filter(.data$y == !!y) %>% select(-y),
                     digits = 3, caption = paste("FY2026 test year:", sev_names[y])))
}
```

How to read this:

-   **Each block helps, in order.** For every severity the log score
    falls as season, conditions, safety and traits are added, so none of
    the blocks from step 03 is dead weight out of sample.
-   **"Same as last year" loses badly on the log score** (about 3.1 vs
    1.7 for all incidents). Last year's count is a noisy guess for one
    beach-month. Its annual-total MAE is reasonable (about 10 incidents
    per beach) because the noise cancels when 12 months are added. It is
    useful as a sanity floor, not as a contender.
-   **Mild (and so all incidents): beach fixed effects win clearly.**
    Log score 1.670 vs 1.710, and the annual miss per beach halves (6.2
    vs 12.6). The five measured traits do not capture everything that
    makes one beach busier with minor incidents than another. Fixed
    effects pick that up.
-   **Close calls: fixed effects edge it in this year** (0.513 vs
    0.521).
-   **Severe: fixed effects fail.** The log score doubles (0.235 vs
    0.109). Many beaches had no severe incident in nine years, so the
    model sets their rate to almost zero. When one then happens, the
    model had given it a probability close to zero, and the log score
    explodes. This is overfitting, and exactly what the log score is
    there to catch: MAE barely notices it (0.258 vs 0.256).
-   **The `v` versions** (free visitor exponent) are slightly better
    than the offset versions with traits, and identical with fixed
    effects. The gain is small (0.003 to 0.012).
-   **Calibration.** Models with traits overpredict mild incidents by
    about 10 to 15% in this year. Fixed effects are within 5%. Every
    model underpredicts severe (ratio about 0.74): 26 happened, about 19
    were expected. Severe incidents are rare enough that one bad year
    moves this a lot, which is why we check other years next.
-   **Top-10 capture for severe.** Our full model puts 46% of severe
    incidents in its top 10 beaches (random would be 12.5%), so the
    ranking is informative even though the total is off.

One test year is one draw. Before choosing, check that the winners hold
up across years.

## 4. Rolling origin

Five folds: test on FY2022, FY2023, FY2024, FY2025 and FY2026, each time
training on every earlier year (an expanding window). FY2021 is not used
as a test year, because the `period_2021` flag would then be estimated
from only one training year.

```{r rolling, results = "asis"}
roll <- bind_rows(lapply(2022:2026, function(f) bind_rows(lapply(names(sev_names), function(y)
  run_split(filter(panel_f, fy < f), filter(panel_f, fy == f), y) %>% mutate(fold = f, y = y)))))

roll_summary <- roll %>% group_by(y, model) %>%
  summarise(nll_mean = mean(nll), nll_sd = sd(nll), mae = mean(mae), ratio = mean(ratio),
            top10 = mean(top10), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(y) %>% arrange(nll_mean, .by_group = TRUE) %>% ungroup()

wins <- roll %>% group_by(y, fold) %>% slice_min(nll, n = 1) %>% ungroup() %>% count(y, model, name = "folds_won")

for (y in names(sev_names)) {
  print(knitr::kable(roll_summary %>% filter(.data$y == !!y) %>% left_join(wins, by = c("y", "model")) %>%
                       mutate(folds_won = coalesce(folds_won, 0L)) %>% select(-y),
                     digits = 4, caption = paste("Rolling origin, 5 folds:", sev_names[y])))
}
```

`nll_sd` is mostly the difference between years (some years are easier
to predict than others), so compare models within a fold, as in the plot
below, rather than reading it as the error of the mean.

```{r rolling_plot, fig.height = 6}
# Log score in each fold, relative to the full traits model (M5), so year-to-year noise drops out
roll %>% filter(model %in% c("M4_safety", "M5_traits", "M5v_slope", "M6_beachFE")) %>%
  group_by(y, fold) %>% mutate(diff = nll - nll[model == "M5_traits"]) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(y = sev_names[y]) %>%
  ggplot(aes(fold, diff, colour = model)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line() + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~y, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.06, 0.06)) +
  labs(x = "test year (FY)", y = "log score minus M5 (below 0 = better than M5)")
```

The plot cuts off the severe fixed-effects line, which sits far above
the others in every fold.

What the folds say:

-   **Mild: a beach fixed-effects model wins every fold** (`M6` and
    `M6v` are tied to four decimals and split the wins; mean log score
    1.61 vs 1.64 for the best model without them), with calibration
    close to 1.00 on average. An easy decision.
-   **Close calls: the full traits model wins on average** (0.537, or
    0.534 with a free visitor exponent) and fixed effects come only
    fifth (0.571). Fixed effects won the two most recent folds but lost
    the first three by more. With about 300 close calls a year spread
    over 80 beaches, 80 beach dummies are too many to estimate well.
    This agrees with the earlier analysis notes.
-   **Severe: the full traits model is the best on average** (0.0878)
    and its total is right on average (ratio 1.00 over five years). The
    winner changes from fold to fold (four different models win at least
    one fold), which is what about 20 events a year looks like. Even the
    winner is only slightly better than simpler models. Fixed effects
    fail in every fold.
-   **Free visitor exponent (`M5v`).** Tied with `M5` for severe and
    0.003 better for close calls. Too small a gain to give up the simple
    reading of "incidents per visitor".

## 5. Decision

**One model per severity, each a negative binomial GLM with
`offset(log(visitors))`:**

| Severity | Model | Decided by | Runner-up |
|----|----|----|----|
| Mild | `M6_beachFE`: season, conditions, safety, visitor mix + **one dummy per beach** | log score; a fixed-effects model won all 5 folds | `M6v` tied (so take the simpler offset version), `M5v` 0.03 worse |
| Close call | `M5_traits`: the step 04 model (season, conditions, safety, visitor mix, beach traits) | mean log score over 5 folds | `M5v` 0.003 better, not worth the extra term, so we take the simpler offset version |
| Severe | `M5_traits` (same as close calls) | mean log score, calibration 1.00 over 5 folds | `M5v` tied; fixed effects overfit badly |

Why this split makes sense: fixed effects need data. Mild incidents
happen about 3,300 times a year, enough to learn each beach's own level.
Close calls and severe incidents are too rare for that, so they borrow
strength across beaches through the measured traits (rips, rocks,
fishing, rockpools, length). That is also the more useful model for Task
2, since it says *why* a beach is risky.

Forecast totals for all incidents are the sum of the three severity
forecasts.

What to tell the panel:

-   The models were chosen on five years they had not seen, not on how
    well they fit the past.
-   For severe incidents the model gets the total right on average, but
    any single year can be off by about a quarter (FY2026: 26 actual vs
    about 19 predicted). Report a range, not a point (step 06).
-   The ranking of risky beaches is more reliable than the count: the
    top 10 beaches hold about 45% of severe incidents, against 12.5% at
    random.

```{r save}
saveRDS(list(mild = specs$M6_beachFE, cc = specs$M5_traits, sev = specs$M5_traits), "part1/chosen_specs.rds")
```
